bib.title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
bib.venue: preprint (DeepMind, arXiv:2203.07814v1 [cs.PL], dated 8 Feb 2022 on the PDF)

question: Can a large transformer code model, with massive sampling and behaviour-based filtering, solve unseen competition-level programming problems at a level competitive with human participants?
hypothesis: Pre-training on GitHub, fine-tuning on competitive programming data, then sampling very many programs and filtering/clustering them by execution behaviour lets a model solve novel problems that need algorithmic reasoning, not copying.
contributions: AlphaCode, a system that pre-trains a transformer on GitHub, fine-tunes on CodeContests, samples up to millions of programs per problem, filters by example tests and clusters by behaviour to at most 10 submissions.
CodeContests, a released training and evaluation dataset with a strict temporal split and generated tests that cut the false positive rate from 62% (raw) to 4%.
Sampling-efficient architecture (asymmetric encoder-decoder with multi-query attention) and training enhancements (MLM, tempering, tags and ratings, value conditioning and prediction, GOLD).
Simulated Codeforces evaluation: average top 54.3% over 10 contests, estimated rating 1238.
Analysis of copying, sensitivity to descriptions and metadata, and validation loss as a poor proxy for solve rate.

method.summary: An encoder-decoder transformer (300M to 41B parameters) is pre-trained on 715.1 GB of GitHub code, then fine-tuned on CodeContests with next-token and masked-LM losses plus tempering, value conditioning/prediction and a GOLD offline-RL objective. At test time up to 1M samples per problem are drawn (half Python, half C++, random tags and ratings), filtered by the example tests (removes >99%), clustered by outputs on model-generated test inputs, and at most 10 are submitted.
method.task: competitive programming code generation from natural-language problem statements (sequence-to-sequence), evaluated by hidden tests

datasets.name: GitHub pre-training snapshot
datasets.source: selected public GitHub repositories, snapshot 2021/07/14; C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Lua, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, TypeScript; licence filtered per Sec 8.2
datasets.preprocessing: dropped files larger than 1MB or with lines longer than 1000 characters; deduplicated files ignoring whitespace

datasets.name: CodeContests
datasets.split: strict temporal: train data public on or before 2021/07/14; valid 2021/07/15 to 2021/09/20; test after 2021/09/21
datasets.source: new Codeforces scrape plus Description2Code (Caballero et al., 2016) and CodeNet (Puri et al., 2021); valid and test are Codeforces only
datasets.preprocessing: Appendix B.2 cleaning (dedupe problems and submissions, C++ reformatting with clang-format, drop submissions passing no tests, tests with under 10% non-empty outputs, submissions passing under 10% of tests); mutation-generated tests verified by 30 correct solutions, max 10 CPU hours or 200 tests per problem; valid/test keep only problems with at least 5 hidden or generated tests giving at least 2 distinct outputs

datasets.name: Codeforces contests Dec 2021
datasets.size: 10 contests with more than 5,000 participants each, 2021/12/01 to 2021/12/28
datasets.source: live Codeforces platform, submissions made after the contests ended (simulated live)
datasets.preprocessing: for problems permitting multiple outputs, example test outputs changed to the most canonical output

datasets.name: APPS
datasets.size: 10,000 problems, equally split train/test (Hendrycks et al., 2021)
datasets.split: official train/test; CodeContests not used because its train set intersects APPS test
datasets.preprocessing: example tests parsed from descriptions with the Figure A4 code; fails for under 2% of test problems

other.purpose: predicts test inputs from problem descriptions, trained on example, hidden and generated test inputs; used only for clustering

other.note: APPS numbers reported from Chen et al. 2021 and Hendrycks et al. 2021

training.objective: Pre-training: next-token cross-entropy for decoder plus masked language modelling for encoder (files split at uniformly sampled pivot, before pivot to encoder, after to decoder). Fine-tuning: same two losses plus tempering (T=0.2), value conditioning and prediction, metadata conditioning, and a GOLD variant (delta-reward offline RL, importance weight max(P^alpha, beta), alpha=1/2, beta=0.05). A short tempering-only phase sits between pre-training and fine-tuning.
training.optimizer: AdamW, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999 for 300M/1B/3B and beta2=0.95 for 9B/41B; global gradient norm clipped to 1.0
training.lr: pre-training initial 1e-4 cosine decayed to 1e-5; fine-tuning initial 1e-5 cosine decayed to 1e-6
training.warmup: linear from 1e-9 to 1e-4 over first 1,000 steps; same 1,000-step warm-up in fine-tuning
training.regularisation: weight decay 0.1; tempering described as a regulariser against overfitting the fine-tuning set
training.hardware: TPUv4 accelerators; JAX and Haiku; 9B and 41B with model parallelism
training.compute: Sec 8.2: 'Both sampling and training from our model required hundreds of petaFLOPS days'; Fig 7 plots training TPU-days (axis only)
training.seeds: Table 8 ablation: at least 3 fine-tuned models per setting from the same pre-trained checkpoint; clustering rows use 5 models; 9B/41B clustering uses single models; no other seed counts given

other.base_1B_pretraining: Sec 4.2 prints '106 steps' (text extraction of 10^6) with batch size 256, matching Table 3 1000k
other.tempering: logits divided by T=0.2 at training; sampling logits divided by T' tuned on validation
other.value_prediction: auxiliary small Transformer on last-layer token representations classifies correct/incorrect; not used at sampling
other.value_conditioning: CORRECT SOLUTION / INCORRECT SOLUTION tag in the prompt; always CORRECT at sampling
other.fine_tuning_data_mix: training split of CodeContests; includes correct and incorrect human submissions in C++, Python, Java

inference.decoding: plain sampling with temperature; top-k and nucleus sampling tried and not better (Fig A5)
inference.temperature: T'=0.25 for tempering+GOLD models, 0.12 for tempering only, tuned separately otherwise; a wide range works (Fig A5 sweeps 0.18 to 0.30)
inference.top_p: not used in main system; nucleus tested at 0.5 to 0.99, best near 1.0; APPS runs use nucleus sampling with temperature 0.25
inference.max_tokens: 768 decoder tokens (Fig 11 caption: 'our samples contain a maximum of 768 tokens')
inference.samples: up to 1,000,000 per problem (Table 5 reaches 10@1M on validation, 10@100k on test); Codeforces: 3 evaluations (reshuffled samples, new clustering inputs and seeds); Table 8 means over at least 3 models with bootstrap CIs
inference.prompting: problem description as encoder input with metadata prefix (RATING, TAGS, LANGUAGE IS, CORRECT SOLUTION); at sampling time rating uniform in 800..3500 step 100, tags drawn at random from the 50 most popular tag combinations, language uniformly C++ or Python, always CORRECT SOLUTION

parameters.filtering: keep samples passing the example tests (removes about 99%); at most 10 submissions
parameters.clustering: 50 generated test inputs, at most 8192 model samples clustered; submit one sample per cluster from largest to smallest cluster, then repeat skipping already-submitted
parameters.judging: float tolerance 1e-5, case-insensitive string comparison, whitespace ignored; multi-output problems judged against the majority human output (about 1/4 of validation problems)
parameters.codeforces_submission_points: Table A4: up to 10 samples clustered and submitted at three points per problem, by fraction of contest time left or by relative number of samples passing example tests; contests assumed 2 hours; 120 s added for clustering

other.ensemble: Codeforces system pooled equal numbers of samples from 41B and 9B before filtering and clustering

metrics.name: n@k
metrics.definition: percentage of problems solved when k samples are drawn per problem and n of them submitted to hidden tests; solved if any submission passes all tests; computed as expectation by sub-sampling k from K>=k samples (Algorithm 1)

metrics.name: pass@k
metrics.definition: k@k; every sample can be submitted; upper bound for k samples

metrics.name: Codeforces percentile ranking
metrics.definition: share of contest participants who placed better than AlphaCode, with simulated submission time and incorrect-submission penalties

metrics.name: estimated Codeforces rating
metrics.definition: Elo-style rating from a reproduction of the Codeforces method over the 10 contests in order, averaged over three evaluations

metrics.name: false positive rate
metrics.definition: share of 50 solved problems (one solution each, manually examined) judged incorrect; 'FP or slow' adds correct but too slow solutions

baselines: decoder-only variant and standard multi-head attention variant of the 1B model
no pre-training, GitHub Python-only, MassiveText pre-training
eval.protocol: CodeContests validation and test with n@k via bootstrapping; Table 8 means and 95% CIs over at least 3 fine-tuned models; Codeforces 10 contests x 3 evaluations (variance from sample ordering and clustering only, models not retrained or resampled); APPS averaged over 3 fine-tuning runs with 3 s time limit per test

availability.code: AlphaCode model code not released; the Figure A4 snippet and dataset tooling in the CodeContests repository

prompts.purpose: encoder input metadata prefix (Fig 5 and Appendix F example)
prompts.text: RATING: 1200 TAGS: dp , implementation LANGUAGE IS python3 CORRECT SOLUTION (then the problem description); C++ form in Appendix F: // RATING: 1200 // TAGS: math // LANGUAGE IS cpp // CORRECT SOLUTION

evidence.quote: Our base 1B parameter model was trained for 106 steps with a batch size of 256.
T′ = 0.12 for models trained with tempering only; T′ = 0.25 for models trained with tempering and GOLD

results.claim: Simulated on 10 Codeforces contests with over 5,000 participants, AlphaCode (41B+9B ensemble with clustering, 10 submissions per problem) ranked in the top 54.3% on average.
results.setup: 41B+9B ensemble, filtering and clustering, at most 10 submissions per problem, Dec 2021 contests, simulated time and penalties, averaged over 3 evaluations in Table 4
results.quote: AlphaCode ranked in the top 54.3% among contest participants averaged over 10 contests
results.note: Table 4 gives Best 48.4% and Worst 77.2% bounds for the same runs

results.claim: Estimated Codeforces rating of 1238, above 72% of users active in the last 6 months.
results.setup: 10 submissions per problem; rating reproduced from the Codeforces Elo method (within 15 points of the real method per Appendix D.3); compared with users who competed in the last 6 months, a self-selected subset
results.quote: achieved an estimated average rating of 1238
results.note: Text says top 28% of users; Fig 1 caption says greater than 72%

results.claim: With more than 10 submissions allowed (still with incorrect-submission penalties) the ranking improves to top 48.8% with 28.8 submissions per solved problem.
results.setup: same system, second and third of three evaluations
results.quote: 48.8%, with an actual average of 28.8 submissions for each problem solved
results.note: Table A6 'Average all' lists 54.3%, 48.8%, 48.4%, 77.2% in its columns

results.claim: 41B with clustering solves 34.2% of CodeContests validation problems with 10 submissions from 1M samples.
results.setup: 41B model; baseline is 41B without clustering (31.8%); the 41B+9B ensemble with clustering reaches 35.5% (Table A2)

results.claim: On the test set, 41B with clustering solves 29.6% with 10 submissions from 100k samples.
results.setup: 41B + clustering vs 41B alone (27.7%); the test set has no 10@1M column
results.quote: 29.6% of problems in our test set

results.claim: Generated tests and filtering cut the CodeContests false positive rate from 62% to 4%.
results.setup: validation split, 1B model solutions, 1,000,000 samples per problem for CodeContests; APPS has 60% and HumanEval 30%; FP-or-slow rate for CodeContests remains 46%

results.claim: Adding the five fine-tuning enhancements raises 10@100k from 15.2% to 24.1% (1B model).
results.setup: 1B encoder-decoder, validation set; build-up of MLM, tempering, tags and ratings, value, GOLD, then clustering; 24.1% is the final row and includes clustering
results.quote: increases the 10@100k solve rate from 15.2% to 24.1%
results.note: Text says 'combining the 5 enhancements'; Table 8 row '+ GOLD' without clustering is 21.5% and '+ Clustering' is 24.1%

results.claim: GOLD (offline RL importance-weighted likelihood) adds a measurable gain on top of value conditioning in the build-up ablation.
results.setup: 1B model, validation set; row '+ GOLD' versus '+ Value'; 95% CIs 20.5-22.2 and 19.6-20.7 overlap slightly
results.note: At 10@1K the gain is larger: 10.6% to 12.4%

results.claim: Behaviour clustering lifts 10@100K from 21.5% to 24.1% and 10@1M from 24.2% to 28.4%, with little effect at 10@1K.
results.setup: 1B model, validation set; clustering uses 50 generated test inputs and 8192 samples
results.table: Table 8, row + Clustering, column 10@100K (24.1% (23.2-25.0)); row + GOLD 21.5%; 10@1M 28.4% vs 24.2%

results.claim: Example-test filtering removes over 99% of samples; less than 1% of samples pass them.
results.metric: fraction of samples passing example tests
results.setup: validation set, models 300M to 41B; Table 9: 41B has at least one passing sample for 92.31% of problems, average p_pass 0.73% over all problems
results.quote: Overall less than 1% of samples from our models pass example tests

results.claim: Solve rate scales approximately log-linearly with number of samples, with larger models having higher slopes.
results.setup: validation set, 300M to 41B, k from 1 to 1M; 10@k curve bends down slightly at high budgets; read from Fig 6

results.claim: Pre-training matters: 10@100K is 10.5% with no pre-training, 21.5% with the full multi-language GitHub dataset.
results.setup: 1B model, validation set; Python-only GitHub 15.5%, MassiveText 21.2%
results.table: Table 7, row GitHub (all languages), column 10@100K; row No pre-training 10.5%

results.claim: Multi-query attention with an asymmetric encoder-decoder samples about 12x faster than standard multi-head attention at similar solve rate.
results.setup: 1B model; standard multi-head attention gets 0.37 samples/TPU sec and 17.0% 10@10K; AlphaCode model 17.3%; decoder-only 1.23 and 18.5%
results.table: Table 6, row AlphaCode model, column Samples / TPU sec (4.74); row Std MH attention 0.37
results.note: 12x is the ratio of the printed 4.74 to 0.37

results.claim: On APPS, AlphaCode 1B with filtering from 50,000 samples and 5 submissions beats Codex 12B (1000 filtered, 5 attempts) on interview and competition levels but not introductory.
results.setup: AlphaCode 1B, k=50000, n=5: introductory 20.36%, interview 9.66%, competition 7.75%; Codex 12B k=1000, n=5: 24.52%, 3.23%, 3.08%; APPS fine-tuning without CodeContests, clustering, tags, ratings or value
results.table: Table 10, rows AlphaCode 1B (50000, 5) and Codex 12B (1000, 5), column Competition n@k

results.claim: A temporal split gives 0% solve rate for a pretrained 1B model with 13k samples per problem, versus 0.8% for a random split.
results.setup: baseline of submitting one training solution per training problem to the validation set: 4.1% random split, 0% temporal split
results.quote: solve rate of 4.1% with a random

results.claim: Validation loss starts to rise after about 50k fine-tuning steps while solve rate keeps improving, so loss is a poor proxy.
results.setup: early 1B fine-tuning run, Fig 13
results.quote: starts increasing after around 50k steps for an early training run of the 1B model

results.claim: Randomising tags per sample gives the best 10@1024 solve rate (1B: 13.5%), better than true tags (13.3%) or random tags fixed per problem (11.9%).
results.setup: 1B model, validation set; 300M 8.2/8.1/6.0, 3B 14.9/13.9/13.3 for the three schemes
results.table: Table 13, row Random per sample (default), column 1B

results.claim: Ensembling 41B and 9B gives 32% (10 submissions) and 35.5% (with clustering) on validation at 1M samples but is not better than 41B alone on test.
results.setup: validation set; test set 41B+9B+clustering 10@100k 29.7% vs 41B+clustering 29.6%, 10@1k 15.6% vs 16.4%

results.claim: Simplifying the problem description raises the share of correct samples sharply (Nim 0.95% to 85.38%), showing the model uses the statement.
results.setup: 1B model, three validation problems and two hand-written
results.table: Table A9, row Nim, column Simplified

results.claim: Large-scale sampling of up to millions of programs per problem is a critical driver of performance.
results.setup: stated design principle of the system

limits: Fixed cost of search: gains need exponentially more samples; 'improving solve rate requires exponentially increasing amounts of samples and the costs quickly become prohibitive' (Sec 5.3.1).
A large gap remains between filtering+clustering and the pass@k upper bound (Fig 8).
CodeContests still accepts slow solutions: FP-or-slow rate is 46% even though false positives are 4% (Table 2); high-difficulty buckets are inflated by this (Appendix E.2).

Judging is permissive and assumes a single correct output for multi-output problems (about 1/4 of validation problems) and does not handle interactive problems, so performance may be under- or over-estimated.

Only 3 evaluations on Codeforces with the same trained models and samples; variance from training and sampling not measured; Codeforces hacking phase not simulated; the 41B model was stopped early and undertrained.
Table 8 ablations are on a single 1B model; larger models mostly have a single run, and most results are from one seed.
Fine-tuning steps, fine-tuning batch size, wall-clock and exact compute are not stated; the training/sampling compute is only shown as axes in Fig 7 and as 'hundreds of petaFLOPS days'.
Codeforces self-selected user group; ranking is of users who have tried competitions.
Encoder-decoder models do worse than decoder-only on HumanEval (Appendix C.5).
Model weights not released; reproduction relies on the released CodeContests dataset only.

terms.definition: percentage of problems solved using n submissions from k samples per problem
solve rate with k samples, all of which can be submitted; pass@k = k@k
dividing the output logits by a scalar temperature T before the softmax at training time; here T=0.2 to sharpen training and smooth inference distribution
inserting a correct/incorrect tag into the prompt and adding an auxiliary classifier of solution correctness
an offline RL algorithm that adds an off-policy importance weight to the maximum likelihood gradient so the model learns from tokens it already assigns high likelihood

lineage.note: offline RL objective used in fine-tuning, in a delta-reward variant
tempering, but with T<1 rather than the suggested T>1
